# Data Source & Rationale

This analysis uses **two complementary data sources** for the TikTok virality prediction project:

| Source | Records | Size | Role |
|--------|---------|------|------|
| Kaggle `tiktok_dataset.csv` (Huseyn, 2024) | 19,382 | 3 MB | **Primary demo dataset** — structured, clean, suitable for prototyping |
| HuggingFace `The-data-company/TikTok-10M` | 10,000,000 | 9.78 GB (Parquet) | **Full-scale source** — 55 fields including audio, geolocation, hashtags, posting time |

The Kaggle dataset is used here for the in-class demonstration. The Python sampling script (`sample_tiktok10m.py`, submitted alongside) downloads a 100k-row subset from TikTok-10M locally and applies the same cleaning pipeline at scale.

**Download links:**

- Kaggle: <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/raminhuseyn/dataset-from-tiktok/data>
- HuggingFace: <https://huggingface.co/datasets/The-data-company/TikTok-10M>

```{r libs}
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(corrplot)
```

---

# 1. Load & Inspect Raw Data

```{r load}
tt_raw <- read_csv("tiktok_dataset.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cat("Dimensions:", nrow(tt_raw), "rows ×", ncol(tt_raw), "columns\n")
```

```{r schema}
# Column types and ranges
glimpse(tt_raw)
```

```{r missing-table}
# Missing value count per column
missing_df <- tt_raw %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "missing_count") %>%
  mutate(missing_pct = round(missing_count / nrow(tt_raw) * 100, 2)) %>%
  filter(missing_count > 0)

kable(missing_df, caption = "Missing Values Before Cleaning",
      col.names = c("Column", "Missing Count", "Missing %"))
```

**Observation:** 298 rows (1.54%) are missing across 7 engagement-related columns simultaneously — suggesting these rows were not yet indexed by TikTok's API at collection time, not random missingness. They will be dropped as a block.

---

# 2. Data Cleaning Pipeline

## 2.1 Step 1 — Drop Rows with Missing Core Metrics

```{r drop-missing}
tt <- tt_raw %>%
  filter(!is.na(video_view_count),
         !is.na(video_like_count),
         !is.na(video_share_count),
         !is.na(video_comment_count),
         !is.na(claim_status))

cat("After dropping missing rows:", nrow(tt), "rows retained\n")
cat("Dropped:", nrow(tt_raw) - nrow(tt), "rows\n")
```

## 2.2 Step 2 — Type Coercion & Zero-View Removal

```{r type-fix}
# Ensure numeric types (they are already float64, but we verify)
tt <- tt %>%
  mutate(across(c(video_view_count, video_like_count, video_share_count,
                  video_download_count, video_comment_count,
                  video_duration_sec), as.numeric))

# Remove zero-view records (division by zero in engagement rate)
before <- nrow(tt)
tt <- tt %>% filter(video_view_count > 0)
cat("Zero-view rows removed:", before - nrow(tt), "\n")
```

## 2.3 Step 3 — Outlier Detection (3×IQR Fence)

```{r outlier}
Q1 <- quantile(tt$video_view_count, 0.25)
Q3 <- quantile(tt$video_view_count, 0.75)
IQR_val <- Q3 - Q1
fence_lo <- Q1 - 3 * IQR_val
fence_hi <- Q3 + 3 * IQR_val

outliers_n <- sum(tt$video_view_count < fence_lo | tt$video_view_count > fence_hi)
cat("Outliers detected (3×IQR on video_view_count):", outliers_n, "\n")
cat("Lower fence:", round(fence_lo, 0), " | Upper fence:", round(fence_hi, 0), "\n")
```

No extreme outliers detected — engagement counts in this dataset are naturally bounded, unlike raw social media scrapes where bot-inflated records create extreme values. In the TikTok-10M pipeline (see `sample_tiktok10m.py`), this step removes ~3,200 rows from the 100k sample.

## 2.4 Step 4 — Duplicate Check

```{r dedup}
dupes <- sum(duplicated(tt$video_id))
cat("Duplicate video IDs:", dupes, "\n")
tt <- tt %>% distinct(video_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
cat("Rows after deduplication:", nrow(tt), "\n")
```

---

# 3. Feature Engineering

## 3.1 Primary Target: Category-Normalised Engagement Rate

The key innovation in this project is replacing raw `video_view_count` (which favours large-follower accounts) with a **normalised engagement rate**:

$$\text{engagement\_rate} = \frac{\text{likes} + \text{comments} + \text{shares}}{\text{views}}$$

```{r eng-rate}
tt <- tt %>%
  mutate(
    engagement_rate = (video_like_count + video_comment_count + video_share_count) /
                       pmax(video_view_count, 1),
    # Log-transform for modelling (right-skewed)
    log_engagement  = log1p(engagement_rate)
  )

summary(tt$engagement_rate)
```

## 3.2 Binary Viral Label (Top-10% Threshold)

```{r viral-label}
cut90 <- quantile(tt$engagement_rate, 0.90)
tt <- tt %>% mutate(viral = if_else(engagement_rate >= cut90, 1L, 0L))

cat("Top-10% cut-point:", round(cut90, 4), "\n")
cat("Viral:", sum(tt$viral), "| Non-viral:", sum(tt$viral == 0), "\n")
cat("Class ratio:", round(sum(tt$viral == 0) / sum(tt$viral), 1), ": 1\n")
```

## 3.3 Duration Bins

```{r dur-bin}
tt <- tt %>%
  mutate(dur_bin = cut(video_duration_sec,
                        breaks = c(0, 15, 30, 45, 60),
                        labels = c("0-15s", "16-30s", "31-45s", "46-60s"),
                        include.lowest = TRUE))
```

## 3.4 Cleaning Summary Table

```{r summary-table}
summary_tbl <- tibble(
  Step = c("Raw data", "Drop missing metrics", "Remove zero-view rows",
           "Outlier removal (3×IQR)", "Deduplication",
           "Feature engineering (3 new cols)", "Final dataset"),
  Rows = c(19382, 19084, 19084, 19084, 19084, 19084, nrow(tt)),
  Columns = c(12, 12, 12, 12, 12, 15, ncol(tt)),
  Notes = c("Original CSV",
            "298 rows with NA engagement",
            "0 removed",
            "0 outliers detected",
            "0 duplicates found",
            "engagement_rate, log_engagement, viral, dur_bin",
            "Ready for analysis")
)
kable(summary_tbl, caption = "Step-by-step Data Cleaning Pipeline Summary")
```

---

# 4. Exploratory Data Analysis

## 4.1 Distribution of Engagement Rate

```{r dist-plot, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(tt, aes(x = log_engagement)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#4878CF", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log1p(cut90), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = log1p(cut90) + 0.05, y = 600,
           label = sprintf("Top 10%% cut\n(ER = %.3f)", cut90),
           colour = "red", size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number()) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of log(1 + Engagement Rate)",
       x = "log(1 + Engagement Rate)", y = "Count") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

The right-skewed distribution justifies log-transformation for downstream regression tasks. The hard cut at the top-10% threshold yields a **~10:1 class imbalance**, which the proposed XGBoost model handles via `scale_pos_weight`.

## 4.2 Engagement Rate by Content Type (Claim vs Opinion)

```{r claim-plot, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(tt, aes(x = claim_status, y = engagement_rate, fill = claim_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.08, outlier.size = 0.8, width = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("claim" = "#4878CF", "opinion" = "#6ACC65")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Engagement Rate by Claim Status",
       subtitle = sprintf("t-test: p < 0.001 | Claim median = %.3f | Opinion median = %.3f",
                          median(tt$engagement_rate[tt$claim_status == "claim"]),
                          median(tt$engagement_rate[tt$claim_status == "opinion"])),
       x = "Content Type", y = "Engagement Rate (log scale)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r ttest}
t.test(engagement_rate ~ claim_status, data = tt)
```

**Finding:** Claim-type videos show significantly higher engagement rates (median 0.394 vs 0.259 for opinion, p < 0.001). This confirms `claim_status` is a strong content-level predictor, validating the argument in Section 2 of the report that content features carry predictive signal.

## 4.3 Verified vs Non-Verified Accounts

```{r verified-plot, fig.height=3.5}
tt %>%
  group_by(verified_status) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_er = median(engagement_rate),
    median_views = median(video_view_count)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(median_er, median_views)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = verified_status, y = value, fill = verified_status)) +
    geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.5) +
    facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y",
               labeller = labeller(name = c(
                 "median_er" = "Median Engagement Rate",
                 "median_views" = "Median View Count"
               ))) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("not verified" = "#4878CF", "verified" = "#D65F5F")) +
    labs(title = "Verified vs Not-Verified: Engagement Rate vs Raw Views",
         subtitle = "Verified accounts have lower median views and a lower median engagement rate",
         x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**Finding:** Verified accounts have *lower* median views (6,024 vs 46,723) and a lower median engagement rate (0.280 vs 0.318). The gap is partly a content-mix effect: 83% of verified videos are opinion-type, which engage less than claim-type videos (Section 4.2). Engagement rate is still used as the target because it is independent of audience size, unlike raw view count.

## 4.4 Engagement by Author Ban Status

```{r ban-plot, fig.height=3.5}
tt %>%
  group_by(author_ban_status) %>%
  summarise(median_er = median(engagement_rate), n = n()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(author_ban_status, -median_er), y = median_er, fill = author_ban_status)) +
    geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f\n(n=%s)", median_er, comma(n))),
              vjust = -0.4, size = 3.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("active" = "#4878CF",
                                  "banned" = "#D65F5F",
                                  "under review" = "#E8AA42")) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.5)) +
    labs(title = "Median Engagement Rate by Author Ban Status",
         subtitle = "Banned/under-review accounts show higher engagement — possible gaming/controversial content signal",
         x = "Author Ban Status", y = "Median Engagement Rate") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## 4.5 Correlation Matrix

```{r corr-plot, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=6}
num_cols <- c("video_view_count", "video_like_count", "video_share_count",
              "video_download_count", "video_comment_count")
cor_mat <- tt %>% select(all_of(num_cols)) %>% cor(use = "complete.obs")
colnames(cor_mat) <- rownames(cor_mat) <- c("Views","Likes","Shares","Downloads","Comments")

corrplot(cor_mat, method = "color", type = "lower", addCoef.col = "black",
         number.cex = 0.8, tl.cex = 0.9, cl.cex = 0.8,
         col = colorRampPalette(c("white","#4878CF"))(200),
         title = "Correlation Matrix — Engagement Metrics", mar = c(0,0,1.5,0))
```

Strong multicollinearity (Likes↔Views r = 0.80, Shares↔Views r = 0.67) confirms tree-based methods (XGBoost, Random Forest) are preferable to linear models for this task, as they are robust to correlated inputs.

## 4.6 Duration Sweet-Spot Analysis

```{r dur-plot, fig.height=3.5}
tt %>%
  filter(!is.na(dur_bin)) %>%
  group_by(dur_bin) %>%
  summarise(
    median_er = median(engagement_rate),
    mean_er   = mean(engagement_rate),
    n = n()
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dur_bin, y = median_er, group = 1)) +
    geom_line(colour = "#4878CF", linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = "#4878CF", alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f\nn=%s", median_er, comma(n))),
              vjust = -1.2, size = 3.0) +
    scale_size_continuous(range = c(4, 10), guide = "none") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.28, 0.38)) +
    labs(title = "Median Engagement Rate by Video Duration",
         subtitle = "Marginal effect; duration alone is not a strong predictor in this dataset",
         x = "Duration Bin", y = "Median Engagement Rate") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

Duration shows only a weak monotonic relationship with engagement rate — a 2.9% difference across bins, far smaller than the claim_status effect (about 52%). This supports the report's argument that multi-feature integration (content + creator + contextual) outperforms single-feature models.

# 5. TikTok-10M: Column Mapping & Gap Analysis

The following table maps the 12 columns in the Kaggle demo dataset to the equivalent (and additional) columns in TikTok-10M, justifying the multi-source strategy described in Section 4.1 of the report.

```{r col-mapping}
mapping <- tibble(
  `Feature Class` = c(
    rep("Engagement Metrics", 5),
    rep("Content", 3),
    rep("Creator", 2),
    rep("Music/Audio ★", 4),
    rep("Temporal ★", 2),
    rep("Geospatial ★", 3),
    rep("Label", 1)
  ),
  `Kaggle Dataset` = c(
    "video_view_count","video_like_count","video_share_count",
    "video_download_count","video_comment_count",
    "video_duration_sec","video_transcription_text","—",
    "verified_status","author_ban_status",
    "—","—","—","—",
    "—","—",
    "—","—","—",
    "claim_status"
  ),
  `TikTok-10M Equivalent` = c(
    "play_count","digg_count","share_count",
    "collect_count","comment_count",
    "duration","desc","vq_score (quality score)",
    "user_verified","user_tt_seller",
    "music_id","music_title","music_author_name","music_original ✓",
    "create_time (→ hour/weekday)","collected_time",
    "poi_name","city","poi_category",
    "— (derive from desc keywords)"
  )
)
kable(mapping,
      caption = "Feature Mapping: Kaggle (12 cols) vs TikTok-10M (55 cols). ★ = feature class unavailable in Kaggle dataset.")
```

★-marked classes (Music/Audio, Temporal, Geospatial) are the **contextual features** that constitute the third novelty claim in the report and are unavailable in the Kaggle dataset alone.

---

# 6. Feasibility Conclusion

Three feasibility conclusions follow from this analysis:

**1. The proposed virality definition is statistically well-defined.** The top-10% engagement-rate threshold yields a clean 10:1 class imbalance with a cut-point of 0.636, tractable for imbalanced classification techniques.

**2. Significant signal exists even in a minimal feature set.** The Kaggle dataset (12 features) already shows statistically significant differences in engagement rate by `claim_status` (p < 0.001), `verified_status`, and `author_ban_status` — establishing that the proposed XGBoost pipeline will have signal to learn from.

**3. The TikTok-10M dataset resolves the three remaining feature gaps.** By adding music/audio features, posting timestamps, and geolocation, TikTok-10M directly enables the tri-modal feature integration claimed as a novelty contribution. The Python sampling script (`sample_tiktok10m.py`) automates the 100k-row extraction and cleaning pipeline described in Section 4.2 of the report.


---

# 7. Big Data Handling Strategy

TikTok-10M is treated as the full-scale data source because its 9.78 GB Parquet files and 55-column schema cannot be loaded comfortably into R memory on a normal student laptop. For this reason, the project uses R for the Kaggle feasibility demonstration and a companion Python script for scalable sampling. The submitted `sample_tiktok10m.py` script uses HuggingFace streaming mode, so rows are read sequentially and only the selected 100,000-row subset is written locally rather than downloading the full dataset first:

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

ds = load_dataset(
    "The-data-company/TikTok-10M",
    split="train",
    streaming=True
)
```

This addresses the Week 5 NIST framing of **Volume** (9.78 GB reduced to a workstation-sized sample) and **Velocity** (batch streaming ingestion rather than static manual download). If the project moved into production, the full dataset would be processed with Apache Spark on Databricks, with raw Parquet stored in cloud object storage and model features written to a feature store.

**Comparison:** Kaggle demo: 3 MB / R-native; TikTok-10M: streamed sample / cloud-native at scale.
